title: Times Square Durga Utsav Draws Crowds Despite Bad Weather, Honours Six Organisations
excerpt: The second annual Sharadiya Durgotsav filled Father Duffy Square with ritual, dance and music on October 10-11, and recognised six diaspora organisations that have sustained Durga Puja in the US for over 50 years.
body:
• The second annual Sharadiya Durga Utsav was held at Father Duffy Square in Times Square on October 10-11, and crowds turned out despite poor weather over the weekend.
  • Six diaspora organisations from California, Illinois, Ohio, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and New York were honoured for championing Durga Puja celebrations for more than 50 years.
  • The two-day programme ran from Chandi Path and Mahalaya songs on Saturday to Maha Ashtami, Maha Navami and Vijaya Dashami pujas, Sindoor Khela and immersion on Sunday.
  • The festival, organised by the Times Square Durga Utsav Association, was first held in 2025, when it drew more than 50,000 visitors over two days, according to its founder.

Times Square hosted Durga Puja for the second year running this weekend, as the Times Square Durga Utsav Association staged its two-day Sharadiya Durgotsav at Father Duffy Square on October 10 and 11. Despite bad weather over the weekend, devotees and onlookers gathered in the middle of Manhattan for rituals, recitations, dance and concerts that brought one of Bengal's biggest festivals to one of the world's busiest public squares.

Two days of ritual and performance

Saturday's programme opened with Chandi Path by Satyam Ray Chowdhury and Mahalaya songs led by Riddhi Bandyopadhyay, followed by rituals from Bodhan through Maha Saptami Puja conducted by priest Prabhas Chakraborty. Children and teenagers raised in New York recited the Gita under the direction of Sutipa Chowdhury, and Sangeet Sadhana Academy, directed by Malabika Chatterjee, presented the inaugural musical performance.

The cultural programme included Dash Mahavidya, a dance production with more than 60 performers from Nrityanjali, choreographed by Chandra Banerjee, and a concert by Mekhla Das Gupta and her troupe. Sunday turned to the Maha Ashtami, Maha Navami and Vijaya Dashami pujas, Pushpanjali and prasad, a Dhunuchi dance by Nrityanjali artists, and closing performances by Diyasini Roy and Jojo Mukherjee and his band, before the festival ended with Sindoor Khela and immersion rituals.

Honouring five decades of puja

A centrepiece of the weekend was the Antorjatik Mahamilon, the international gathering session presided over by Mridul Pathak and moderated by Dr. Kallol Basu. During the session, the association honoured six diaspora organisations from across the United States - drawn from California, Illinois, Ohio, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and New York - that have kept Durga Puja celebrations going for more than 50 years. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Consuls General of India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Thailand were among the dignitaries recognised as supporters of the celebration.

The association is led by president Shashadhar Howlader, with Biswajit Saha as its founder and Nirupama Saha as general secretary. Saha has described the Dhunuchi dance - performed with a burning earthen pot held in the hands, and sometimes in the teeth - as a demanding devotional offering that symbolises the Goddess's victory over evil and the removal of negative energies.

Why it matters for the community

For Bengali families in the New York area, the festival does work that a neighbourhood pandal cannot: it places their tradition in full public view, in a space shared with the whole city. Organisers say the celebration has grown into a gathering point for Bengalis of different regions and backgrounds, and community leaders at the launch noted that Bangladeshi Hindus in New York have been celebrating Durga Puja since the early 1990s. Holding the rituals to the traditional calendar, with a priest conducting each stage in sequence, is central to that appeal for families raising children in the diaspora.

What comes next

With two editions now complete, the association presents the Times Square puja as an annual fixture rather than a one-off spectacle, and organisers say each year is a chance to deepen its role as a devotional gathering and a public celebration of South Asian heritage in New York. Devotees who missed the weekend can still catch the wider Diwali season across the tri-state area in the coming weeks.
